items.prompt: Which command lists the positions a ref has pointed to over time?
choices: git log
git status
git blame
git reflog
items.explanation: The reflog is the per-ref diary of positions.

items.prompt: What does git log show?
choices: Every position that HEAD has ever occupied
Commits reachable from where a ref points now
Only your uncommitted edits in the working tree
Only commits made by you in the last day
items.explanation: It walks parent links backward from the current tip.

items.prompt: After reset --hard moves a branch back, does git log still list the commits it moved past?
choices: Yes, in a separate section at the bottom
Yes, but marked as abandoned commits in grey
Only if you pass a flag that hides merge commits
No, they are no longer reachable from the branch
items.explanation: They are off the walk, even though they are stored.

items.prompt: Where does the reflog live?
choices: On the remote server, next to the branches
In your local .git directory
Inside the text of each commit message
In a shared team file that is pushed
items.explanation: It is a local record.

items.prompt: What is a ref?
choices: A named pointer to a commit, such as a branch, tag or HEAD
A full copy of the files in one commit
A backup of the whole repository on disk
A list of every author who has committed
items.explanation: Refs are the labels git walks from.

items.prompt: Which tells you how you arrived at the current state?
choices: The staging area
A tag name
The reflog
The commit author field
items.explanation: It records each move, with a reason.

items.prompt: What is a dangling commit?
choices: A commit that was written without any message
A stored commit that no ref currently reaches
A commit that failed to push to the remote
A commit that has been merged into two branches
items.explanation: It exists in the object store but is unreachable.

items.prompt: Reflog entries are numbered. Which entry is the newest?
choices: The highest number
Number 1
Whichever has a tag
Number 0
items.explanation: Zero is the current position; higher numbers are older.

items.prompt: After reset --hard B, you want to see that commits C and D once existed. Which command can show them?
choices: git log, because it prints every commit in the object store
git status, because it compares HEAD with the index
git log --all, because it lists abandoned commits with no ref
git reflog, because it records the earlier positions of HEAD
items.explanation: Only the reflog keeps old positions; --all still needs a ref to reach them.
items.reference:
Two views of the same repo
📜 git log: walks back from where a ref points now
🕰️ git reflog: lists where a ref pointed, newest first
👻 After a reset, lost commits show only in the reflog
Why: log describes the current graph; reflog describes how you got here.
items.learnMore:
Graph vs. timeline

git log follows parent links from the current tip, so anything the tip no longer leads to disappears from it. The reflog is a separate list of positions, one entry per move of the ref, and it does not care about reachability.

Common mistake

Expecting git log to show everything git still stores.
items.reflection: Think of a browser: the page you are on has links back to earlier pages, but the history menu lists every page you visited, including ones you left. Which of those two would you use to find a tab you closed by accident?

items.prompt: A colleague says: 'git log and git reflog are the same list, just formatted differently.' What is wrong with that?
choices: reflog is sorted by author name while log is sorted by date
log only shows merge commits while reflog shows every kind of commit
log follows parent links from a tip; reflog lists past positions in order, even unreachable ones
reflog is read from the remote while log is read from your own disk
items.explanation: They answer different questions: ancestry versus movement.

choices: One entry per move of HEAD: the switches and the commits
Only the two commits you made that day, nothing else
Only the five branch switches, but not the commits

items.prompt: What does git reset --hard do to commit objects?
choices: Deletes them immediately from the object store
Nothing; it moves the branch pointer
Compresses them into a single archive file
Copies them to the remote as a safety measure
items.explanation: Objects stay in the object store.

items.prompt: After a reset, the old commits are called what?
choices: Merged into the branch you reset to
Rebased onto the branch you reset to
Tagged with an automatic backup name
Unreachable (dangling)
items.explanation: No ref leads to them any more.

items.prompt: Which command actually removes unreachable objects?
choices: git gc (after expiry)
git status, after the expiry window passes
git log, run with the prune option
git reset --soft, run a second time
items.explanation: Pruning happens in garbage collection.

items.prompt: Is a reset of committed work usually recoverable?
choices: No, never
Only on the remote
Yes, via the reflog
Only within one minute
items.explanation: The reflog points at the old tip.

items.prompt: What does the 'hard' in --hard refer to?
choices: Deleting the commits from the object store
Asking for a password before the reset runs
Also overwriting the index and working files
Resetting the remote branch as well
items.explanation: It changes more layers than --soft or --mixed.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT removed from the object store by git branch -D?
choices: The commits the branch pointed to
The branch label (the name) itself
The branch's own reflog file
The pointer file under refs/heads
items.explanation: Only the label (and its log) go.

items.prompt: A teammate shouts 'I deleted my commits!' after a reset. What is the best first question?
choices: Which editor were you using?
Have you restarted the computer?
Is the remote up to date?
Were the changes ever committed?
items.explanation: Committed work survives; uncommitted edits do not.

items.prompt: Which command moves a branch pointer without touching your files?
choices: git reset --hard
git reset --soft
git checkout .
git clean -f
items.explanation: --soft moves only the pointer.

items.prompt: You ran git reset --hard HEAD~3 ten minutes ago. What is the state of the three dropped commits?
choices: Still stored, unreachable from the branch, listed in the HEAD reflog
Deleted, though git keeps their messages in a separate log
Moved to a hidden stash that expires in about an hour
Stored only on the remote, with no local copy left
items.explanation: Reset never deleted them; gc has not run past the expiry windows.
items.reference:
What reset --hard really does
➡️ Moves the branch pointer to the target
📁 Rewrites index and files to match it
🗃️ Leaves the old commit objects in .git
🧹 Only gc can delete them, later
Why: A pointer move is not a deletion.
items.learnMore:
Pointer vs. object

A commit is an object stored under .git/objects; a branch is a small file holding a hash. Reset edits the file, not the object. Objects go away only when nothing references them and gc prunes them after the expiry windows.

Common mistake

Believing the word 'hard' means the commits are erased.
items.reflection: Some tools really do erase: shredding a paper file versus moving a bookmark. For a mistake you made last week in git, how would you decide which one happened before you panic?

items.prompt: Which scenario loses data that the reflog cannot bring back?
choices: Editing a tracked file without ever staging or committing it, then running reset --hard
Committing twice, then running reset --hard HEAD~2 afterwards
Rebasing a branch and then finding the result is wrong
Deleting a branch after you switched away from it
items.explanation: Uncommitted edits never became objects.

The remote has overwritten the local history during fetch
The commits were garbage collected and fsck found only fragments
The commits are unreachable but still stored, so they are recoverable

items.prompt: In a reflog line, what does the first column hold?
choices: The name of the person who made the move
The name of the branch that HEAD was on
The list of files touched by the move
The commit id HEAD pointed to
items.explanation: Each line starts with a (shortened) hash.

items.prompt: Which entry is 'where HEAD is right now'?
choices: The oldest entry
HEAD at-position-zero
The entry with the longest message
The last pushed entry
items.explanation: Index zero is the current position.

items.prompt: What does the word after the position, like 'commit:' or 'reset:', tell you?
choices: What kind of operation moved HEAD
Who ran the command that caused the move
Which remote the command talked to
Which file the command changed last
items.explanation: The reason is recorded per move.

items.prompt: Which notation follows parent links?
choices: HEAD at one in braces
ORIG_HEAD
HEAD~1
FETCH_HEAD
items.explanation: Tilde walks ancestry.

items.prompt: What does HEAD@{2.days.ago} mean?
choices: The commit two parents back from the tip
Where HEAD pointed two days ago on this machine
The tag that was created two days ago
The tip of the remote branch two days ago
items.explanation: Time-based reflog lookups are local.

items.prompt: What does ORIG_HEAD usually hold?
choices: The very first commit ever made in the repository
The current HEAD of the remote repository
The newest tag that was created locally
HEAD's value before a risky operation like reset, merge or rebase
items.explanation: It is a one-step undo pointer.

items.prompt: Which gives a branch's own history of positions, not HEAD's?
choices: git reflog show main
git log main, which lists only reachable commits
git branch -v, which lists branch tips
git show main, which prints one commit
items.explanation: Each ref can have its own reflog.

items.prompt: Do the position numbers stay fixed over time?
choices: Yes, they are permanent labels for each entry
Only for branches, but not for HEAD
No, they shift as new entries are added
Only until the next time gc has run
items.explanation: They are relative to the newest entry.

items.prompt: After 'git reset --hard B', you want the tip you just left. Which expression names it?
choices: HEAD at one-in-braces (the previous position of HEAD)
HEAD~1, which is the parent of B
HEAD^2, the second parent of B, if it has one
FETCH_HEAD, the tip of the last fetch
items.explanation: HEAD~1 is B's parent; the old tip is the previous reflog position.
items.reference:
Anatomy of one entry
🔖 e7c9d14: the commit id at that moment
🔢 HEAD@{1}: one move ago (0 = now)
🏷️ commit / reset / pull: why it moved
🆚 HEAD~1 follows parents, not moves
Why: @ navigates time; ~ navigates ancestry.
items.learnMore:
Two ways to say 'before'

HEAD~N walks N parent links from the current commit, so it describes the graph. HEAD@ followed by a number in braces counts back through the reflog, so it describes your own recent history, including positions that are no longer ancestors.

Common mistake

Using HEAD~1 to find a commit that a reset moved past: it is not an ancestor any more.
items.reflection: You have a shell history and a browser history. If you wanted to reopen something you saw yesterday, what clue would you use to choose between 'the previous page by links' and 'the previous page by time'?

choices: It disappears from the reflog

The id is stable; the position changes with every new move
Ids are shorter to type than positions in braces

items.prompt: By default, how long do reflog entries for reachable commits last?
choices: 1 day
7 days
Forever
90 days
items.explanation: gc.reflogExpire defaults to 90 days.

items.prompt: By default, how long do entries for unreachable commits last?
choices: 90 days
30 days
2 hours
Forever
items.explanation: gc.reflogExpireUnreachable defaults to 30 days.

items.prompt: Which command prunes unreachable objects?
choices: git log
git switch
git diff
git gc
items.explanation: Garbage collection is the real delete step.

items.prompt: Can gc run without you typing it?
choices: No, it only runs when you type it yourself
Yes, git can trigger it automatically
Only on Fridays, when the repository is idle
Only on the remote, never on your clone
items.explanation: Auto gc runs after some commands.

items.prompt: Is a reset from two days ago close to the expiry windows?
choices: No, it is far inside them
Yes, it is nearly expired
It expires in an hour
It already expired
items.explanation: Two days is tiny against 30 or 90.

items.prompt: Which setting names the 30-day clock?
choices: gc.reflogExpire, which is the 90-day clock
core.editor, which names your text editor
gc.reflogExpireUnreachable
user.email, which names the author address
items.explanation: Unreachable entries get the shorter clock.

items.prompt: What is the 'point of no return' for a lost commit?
choices: Running git status after the window ends
gc pruning it after expiry
Switching to another branch and back
Making one more commit on top of it
items.explanation: After that, no object remains.

items.prompt: What should you avoid right after a mistake?
choices: Reading the reflog to find the old tip
Creating a new branch at the old tip
Waiting a few minutes before deciding
Running more history-rewriting commands on top of it
items.explanation: Urgency is about not complicating things.

items.prompt: You reset away 3 commits 45 days ago and never ran gc. What is most likely true?
choices: Everything is safe, because the default is 90 days for all entries
They were already pushed, so the reflog entry no longer matters
They stay protected until you run git reflog expire yourself
Their reflog entries (unreachable, 30 days) have expired, so gc may now prune them
items.explanation: Unreachable commits use the shorter 30-day clock; after it, gc is free to delete.
items.reference:
Two clocks
⏳ Reflog entry expires: 90 days reachable, 30 days unreachable
🧹 gc prunes objects with no ref and no live entry
🛟 Until both: recoverable
Why: Time plus gc decide when it is really gone.
items.learnMore:
Defaults and knobs

gc.reflogExpire (90 days) and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (30 days) set how long entries live. gc.pruneExpire (2 weeks) is a grace period before unreachable loose objects are deleted. Automatic gc can run after commands, so do not assume it never will.

Common mistake

Assuming recovery is still possible months later because the objects were never explicitly deleted.
items.reflection: Smoke detectors and expiry dates on a medicine cabinet both give you a window to act. Who in your team decides how long such a window needs to be, and what would happen if CI machines set it to zero?

items.prompt: Which pair of conditions must both hold before a lost commit's object is actually deleted?
choices: The commit is older than two weeks and has no tag on it
The commit was never pushed and its branch was deleted
No live reflog entry or ref reaches it, and gc runs after the grace period
A teammate has run git push --force on the same branch
items.explanation: Both reachability and expiry matter.

Nothing important; it only tidies the remote's refs
It extends the recovery window to 180 days for safety
It only affects tags, so commits stay recoverable

items.prompt: Is the reflog shared with teammates on push?
choices: Yes, it is pushed together with every branch
Yes, but only for tags you created
Yes, but only for the main branch
No, it is local only
items.explanation: It never leaves your .git.

items.prompt: Does a fresh clone include the original repo's reflog?
choices: Yes, in full, copied from the source
No, it starts empty
Yes, but trimmed to the last thirty days
Yes, but only the entries for HEAD
items.explanation: Reflogs are not transferred.

items.prompt: Can the reflog restore edits you never committed?
choices: Yes, up to 90 days
Yes, if staged
Yes, if saved in an editor
No
items.explanation: It tracks commits and ref moves, not file edits.

items.prompt: Which tracks moves per ref?
choices: One global log for the repo
Each ref has its own reflog
Only HEAD has one
Only remote refs have one
items.explanation: Branches, HEAD and remote-tracking refs each keep a log.

items.prompt: What happens to a branch's own reflog when you delete the branch?
choices: It is deleted with it
It is archived
It moves to HEAD
It is pushed to the remote
items.explanation: Log files go with the ref.

items.prompt: Where can you still find the old tip after git branch -D?
choices: On the remote only, in its server logs
In the staging area of your clone
In HEAD's reflog, if HEAD had been on that branch
In the .gitignore file at the root
items.explanation: HEAD's log keeps its own history.

items.prompt: After a force-push overwrote the remote, your local origin/main reflog holds what?
choices: Nothing at all, because remote refs have no logs
The old tip, if you fetched before the overwrite
Your teammates' stashes from their machines
The remote server's own access logs
items.explanation: Fetches update the local remote-tracking ref and its log.

items.prompt: Which command may dig out staged-but-never-committed file contents?
choices: git reflog, which lists only committed moves
git log -p, which shows patches of reachable commits
git blame, which shows who wrote each line
git fsck --lost-found
items.explanation: Staging wrote blobs into the object store.

items.prompt: Your teammate force-pushed over main and lost two commits that you never fetched. Can your reflog restore them?
choices: Yes, by reading HEAD at-two in your own reflog
Yes, through the remote's reflog stored in your clone
Yes, but only after you run git gc once
No; they never passed through your repository
items.explanation: A reflog only records what happened in this clone.
items.reference:
What the reflog cannot save
✏️ Edits never committed
🌐 Other people's machines
🆕 A fresh clone
🌿 A deleted branch's own log
Why: Local, per-ref, and commit-based.
items.learnMore:
Local and per-ref

Every ref has its own reflog in your .git, updated by your own commands. Nothing is pushed or cloned. Deleting a branch deletes that branch's log, which is why recovery often goes through HEAD's log instead. Remote-tracking refs like origin/main have logs too, updated on fetch.

Common mistake

Asking a coworker to look in their reflog for your lost commits, or vice versa.
items.reflection: Your phone's recent-calls list only knows calls on your phone. If a friend lost their call history, would your list help? When might it?

The stash list, where deleted branches are parked
items.explanation: The branch's own log is gone; a remote-tracking ref may remember the tip.

items.prompt: What does git bisect do?
choices: Recovers deleted commits from the reflog
Merges two long-running branches together
Shows which author wrote each line of a file
Binary-searches history for the first bad commit
items.explanation: It narrows a good/bad range by halving.

items.prompt: What do you give bisect to start?
choices: One good commit and one bad commit
A branch name and nothing else
A list of authors to include in the search
A date range for the history to scan
items.explanation: The two ends of the range.

items.prompt: About how many tests do 500 commits need?
choices: About 500
About 250
About 9
About 50
items.explanation: ceil of log2(500) is 9.

items.prompt: Which commit does bisect check out for you to test?

A randomly chosen commit from the range
The midpoint of the remaining range
The oldest commit in the remaining range

items.prompt: If the midpoint is bad, which half is kept?
choices: The earlier half, including the midpoint
The later half, after the midpoint
Both halves, to be safe
Neither half; the search ends there

items.prompt: If the midpoint is good, which half is kept?

Both halves, to stay safe
Neither half; the session is over
The later half, after the midpoint

items.prompt: How do you end a bisect session and return to your branch?

git reset --bisect
git checkout --end

items.prompt: Does bisect fix the bug it finds?

Yes, by reverting the commit it finds
Only for bugs that touch a single line
No, it only identifies the first bad commit

items.prompt: A range has 1000 commits between good and bad. Roughly how many tests will bisect need?

About 500
About 10
About 31
items.explanation: ceil of log2(1000) is 10.
items.reference:
Halving the range
🟢 good commit at the start
🔴 bad commit at the end
🎯 test the midpoint, keep the half that must hold the flip
📉 about log2(n) tests for n commits
Why: Each answer halves the search space.
items.learnMore:
Why log2

If each test discards half of the remaining commits, the number of tests is the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1: ceil(log2(n)). 500 commits: 9. 2000 commits: 11.

Common mistake

Thinking a bad midpoint means the midpoint itself is guilty.

items.prompt: Where do you look for the hash of lost commits?
choices: git log
git diff
git reflog
git stash list
items.explanation: The reflog lists old tips.

items.prompt: What command makes a branch at an old commit id?
choices: git delete recovery followed by the commit id
git branch recovery followed by the old commit id
git merge recovery followed by the commit id
git tag --remove followed by the commit id
items.explanation: A branch is just a name for a commit.

items.prompt: Why create a branch before resetting?
choices: To make later git commands run faster
To delete the reflog before it expires
To push the lost work to the remote first
To pin the old tip with a stable name
items.explanation: A name does not shift like an index.

items.prompt: How can you check the right work was found?
choices: git log on the new branch
git gc, to clean the object store
git clean, to remove untracked files
git rebase, to replay the commits
items.explanation: Inspect before restoring.

items.prompt: Which command moves your current branch to the recovered tip?
choices: git reflog expire, to drop old entries
git bisect good, to mark the commit
git reset --hard recovery
git fetch, to refresh the remote
items.explanation: Once confirmed, move the pointer.

items.prompt: Instead of resetting, which lets you keep your current work and add the lost commits?
choices: git gc, to prune the object store
git stash drop, to discard saved work
git merge recovery
git clean, to remove untracked files
items.explanation: Merging combines both lines.

items.prompt: Which command copies just one lost commit onto your branch?
choices: git cherry-pick followed by the commit id
git revert --all, which undoes every commit
git blame, which annotates each line
git archive, which packs files into a tarball
items.explanation: Cherry-pick applies a single commit.

items.prompt: Does creating a recovery branch change your working files?
choices: Yes, it overwrites them
Yes, it deletes untracked files
Yes, it resets the index
No, it only adds a name
items.explanation: git branch does not check anything out.

items.prompt: You found the lost tip as the second entry of the reflog. Which first command is safest?
choices: git reset --hard HEAD at-two, straight to the index
git gc --prune=now, to tidy up before recovering
git reflog delete on the entry, to avoid confusion
git branch recovery followed by the commit id
items.explanation: Anchor before any destructive move; reset could use the wrong index.
items.reference:
Recovery order
1️⃣ git reflog: find the old tip
2️⃣ git branch recovery <id>: anchor it
3️⃣ git log recovery: check it
4️⃣ reset --hard / merge / cherry-pick
Why: Anchor before you move anything.
items.learnMore:
Anchor first

A branch is a stable name; a reflog position is a moving index. Creating a branch at the old tip costs one command and guarantees that later mistakes cannot lose the only handle. After that you choose how to bring the work back: reset the branch, merge it, or cherry-pick pieces.

Common mistake

Running reset --hard HEAD at-one-in-braces twice and landing on a different commit the second time.

Reflog entries drop random commits from time to time

items.prompt: What does 'git bisect skip' do?
choices: Marks the commit as good and moves on
Marks the commit as bad and moves on
Deletes the commit from the history
Marks a commit as untestable and moves on
items.explanation: For commits that do not build.

items.prompt: What does exit code 0 mean to git bisect run?
choices: The commit is bad
The commit is good
Skip the commit
Abort the session
items.explanation: Zero is success.

items.prompt: What does exit code 125 mean to git bisect run?
choices: Mark it as good, keep searching
Mark it as bad, keep searching
Stop the whole session immediately
Skip this commit
items.explanation: 125 is the reserved skip code.

items.prompt: What does a nonzero exit like 1 mean to bisect run?
choices: The commit is good
The commit is bad
Skip this commit
Retry the same commit once more
items.explanation: Codes 1 to 127 except 125 mean bad.

items.prompt: Bisect assumes how many good-to-bad flips?
choices: One
Two
As many as commits
Zero
items.explanation: A single transition.

items.prompt: What if your test passes sometimes and fails sometimes on the same commit?
choices: Bisect detects it and retries automatically
It proves that the commit is bad
It is flaky and can mislead bisect
It forces git to skip the commit
items.explanation: Bisect trusts each answer.

items.prompt: Which command shows the record of your good and bad answers?
choices: git bisect map
git bisect log
git reflog
git blame
items.explanation: The log can be saved and replayed.

items.prompt: Is HEAD detached during a bisect?
choices: No, it stays on main throughout the session
Only at the start, before the first answer
Only at the end, after the culprit is found
Yes, at the candidate commit
items.explanation: Bisect checks out candidates directly.

items.prompt: A regression was fixed in commit 300 and reintroduced in commit 450. Bisecting the whole 1 to 500 range may do what?
choices: Stop with an error saying two flips were found
Always return commit 450, the later flip
Always return commit 300, the earlier flip
Land on either flip, depending on where midpoints fall
items.explanation: The halving assumes a single transition and does not detect more.
items.reference:
When halving misleads
🔁 Fixed then reintroduced: two flips
🎲 Flaky test: one wrong answer, wrong half
🚧 Won't build: git bisect skip
🤖 bisect run: exit 0 good, 125 skip, 1-127 bad
Why: Bisect trusts that your oracle is reliable and monotone.
items.learnMore:
The oracle assumption

Binary search needs a single good-to-bad transition and a trustworthy test. If those fail, bisect still prints a confident answer. You protect it by making the test deterministic, skipping untestable commits, and bisecting each flip separately.

Common mistake

Trusting the first bad commit without checking that it really causes the symptom.
items.reflection: A thermometer that sometimes reads wrong would send a doctor to the wrong ward. In your own work, what 'thermometer' do you rely on that might sometimes lie, and how would you notice?

Disable the flaky test for the affected commits
Run the test several times per candidate, and only mark bad on repeated failures
Only test odd-numbered commits to reduce noise
items.explanation: A single false answer can send the search the wrong way.
